questions.question: What did the author do to arrive at this recipe for doing great work?
questions.referenceAnswer: He collected lists of techniques for doing great work from many different fields and looked at what they had in common, i.e. their intersection.

questions.question: What three qualities does the article say the work you choose to do must have?
questions.referenceAnswer: It has to be something you have a natural aptitude for, that you have a deep interest in, and that offers scope to do great work.

questions.premise: The article says the work you choose needs to be something you have aptitude for, deep interest in, and that offers scope for great work.
questions.question: What kind of curiosity does the article say marks the deep interest you should be looking for?
questions.referenceAnswer: An excessive curiosity - curiosity about something to a degree that would bore most other people.

questions.premise: The interest you're looking for is an excessive curiosity, one that would bore most other people.
questions.question: What four steps does the article lay out as the way practically everyone who's done great work has done it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Choose a field, learn enough to get to the frontier of knowledge in it, notice the gaps in that frontier, and explore the promising ones.

questions.premise: The four steps are choosing a field, learning enough to reach its frontier, noticing the gaps in it, and exploring the promising ones.
questions.question: Instead of making and executing a plan, what does the article say the recipe for doing great work usually is?
questions.referenceAnswer: Work hard on excitingly ambitious projects while just trying to preserve certain invariants, an approach the author calls 'staying upwind': at each stage doing whatever seems most interesting and gives the best future options.

questions.question: Why does the article say it's acceptable to lie to yourself when starting work or a new project?
questions.referenceAnswer: Because work has an 'activation energy' that's higher than what's needed to keep going, so a small lie, such as telling yourself you're just going to glance at what you've done or underestimating how much a project will take, helps you get over that initial threshold.

questions.question: What's the key difference the article draws between per-day procrastination and per-project procrastination?
questions.referenceAnswer: Per-project procrastination, putting off an ambitious project for years, is far more dangerous because it disguises itself as work: you're busy doing something else, so it doesn't set off the alarm that daily procrastination does.

questions.premise: Per-project procrastination is more dangerous because it disguises itself as being busy with other work.
questions.question: What does the article say actually distinguishes people who accomplish great amounts of work over time?
questions.referenceAnswer: They don't necessarily get a lot done every day; they get something done each day rather than nothing, and that consistency compounds into large achievements over time.

questions.question: What does the article say happens to your work if you don't try to be the best in your field?
questions.referenceAnswer: You won't even end up being good; trying to be the best is what's actually required just to be good.

questions.premise: If you don't try to be the best, you won't even end up being good.
questions.question: How does the article define affectation, the thing you should avoid?
questions.referenceAnswer: Affectation is effectively pretending that someone other than you is doing the work, adopting an impressive but fake persona, so that the fakeness ends up showing in the work.

questions.premise: Affectation means pretending someone other than you is doing the work, by adopting a fake, impressive persona.
questions.question: What quality does the article recommend as the positive alternative to avoiding affectation?
questions.referenceAnswer: Being earnest, whose core is being intellectually honest.

questions.question: When work could be seen as either creation or discovery, what does the article say you should do?
questions.referenceAnswer: Err on the side of discovery, trying to think of yourself as a mere conduit through which the ideas take their natural shape.

questions.question: According to the article, where do original ideas actually come from, rather than from directly trying to have them?
questions.referenceAnswer: From trying to build or understand something slightly too difficult for you.

questions.premise: Original ideas come from trying to build or understand something slightly too difficult for you.
questions.question: What two qualities does the article say you need together in order to notice and fix a broken model of the world?
questions.referenceAnswer: Strictness, being stricter than other people about noticing where reality clashes with the accepted model, combined with a willingness to break rules.

questions.question: What does the article say matters even more than originality in solving problems?
questions.referenceAnswer: Originality in choosing which problem to work on in the first place; this is what distinguishes the people who discover whole new fields.

questions.premise: Originality in choosing which problem to work on matters even more than originality in solving it.
questions.question: How does the article say you get from starting small to eventually doing something great?
questions.referenceAnswer: By making successive versions: you start with something small and evolve it, so the final version ends up cleverer and more ambitious than anything you could have planned.

questions.premise: You get from starting small to doing something great by making successive versions, starting small and evolving it.
questions.question: What does the article say you should do about risk when working on ambitious projects?
questions.referenceAnswer: Take as much risk as you can afford, looking for a bet with high expected value rather than certainty; if you're not failing occasionally, you're probably being too conservative.

questions.question: What's the difference between the good way and the bad way of copying other people's work, according to the article?
questions.referenceAnswer: The good way is to copy openly and consciously; the bad way is to copy furtively or unconsciously, which reduces you to nothing more than a train running on tracks laid down by someone else.

questions.question: What does the article say matters more when it comes to colleagues, their quality or their quantity?
questions.referenceAnswer: Quality matters more; it's better to have one or two great colleagues than a building full of merely pretty good ones.

questions.question: What four factors does the article say determine whether you do great work?
questions.referenceAnswer: Ability, interest, effort, and luck.
